q7.answer: Presence lives in Redis, per document and per connection (connId), not per user. A ZSET pres:z:{doc} holds each connId with an expiry score (Redis TIME + 30 s). HASH pres:i:{doc} holds who the connection is, and HASH pres:c:{doc} holds its last cursor. Each node also keeps the truth in memory and refreshes its connections every 10 s with a REFRESH script, which re-writes the entries. All three keys also have EXPIRE 90.

q8.answer: Nothing is told by the dead node. Its entries stay in Redis until their score expires (at most 30 s after the crash). Then the SWEEP script, which every live node runs every 5 s for its documents, removes them and publishes conn_left on pres:{doc} atomically with the removal. Other nodes forward it to their clients, with userGone true if that was the user's last connection. About 35 s in total, under the 45 s limit. If no node is left in the doc, the 90 s EXPIRE deletes the keys.

q9.answer: The CURSOR script writes the cursor to pres:c:{doc} and publishes it on pres:{doc} in the same call. Every node subscribed to pres:{doc} receives it and sends it to all its local sockets of that doc except the sender's own connId. So viewers on other nodes get it through the pub/sub fan-out, and viewers on the sender's own node (including the sender's other tabs) get it from the same pub/sub message, not by a local shortcut.

q10.answer: The node subscribes to pres:{doc} before running the JOIN script that returns the snapshot. Events arriving before the snapshot is sent are held by the node for that connection and sent right after it. The client applies them through the seq guard, and joins and leaves are idempotent set operations, so overlap with the snapshot is harmless. The 5 s sweep compare also repairs anything lost.

q11.answer: Each connection's last cursor is stored in the Redis HASH pres:c:{doc}, and the JOIN snapshot returns all of them, so an idle user's caret is delivered as stored state and not as a stream. The node re-writes each cursor from its memory on every 10 s heartbeat, and a client re-sends its cursor on a 10 s timer when appliedRev has moved, so the stored position stays inside the 500-revision history that transformPosition needs.

q12.answer: Ordering uses the sender's own per-connection seq, not arrival order or revision. The receiver keeps lastSeq per connId and ignores any cursor with seq less than or equal to it. A held cursor has one slot per connId holding the highest seq. Cursors from a reconnect have a new connId, so a restarted seq cannot clash with the old one.
